labels.text: Search Results: STANDARD M10 and other index tests
We screened 34 titles and abstracts and excluded 32. We assessed the full texts of two articles and
found none eligible for this review (Figure 3).
Figure 3.  Study flow diagram for STANDARD M10 and other new LC-aNAATs
Characteristics of included studies
There were 36 included studies: 31 that only evaluated Xpert Ultra (including one study based on two
reports—Nicol 2018 and Zar 2019—and two studies extracted from a single report—Mishra 2020a &
2020b), three studies that only evaluated Truenat MTB Plus (Gomathi 2020, Jose 2024, Ngangue
2022), and two studies that evaluated both tests (Penn-Nicholson 2021, Theron 2024). Key
characteristics of the studies are described in Table 1 (Xpert Ultra) and Table 2 (Truenat MTB Plus).
Thirty-four studies assessed LC-aNAATs (Xpert Ultra, Truenat MTB Plus) for detection of PTB using a
microbiological reference standard. One multicentre study (Penn-Nicholson 2021) compared the
accuracy of Truenat MTB Plus (multiple countries) and Xpert Ultra (only in Peru). Theron 2024
evaluated both Xpert Ultra and Truenat MTB Plus in South Africa.
Adolescents (10-14 years) were included in 12 studies, of which 11 evaluated Xpert Ultra and one
study (Jose 2024) evaluated Truenat MTB Plus. Seven of these studies included adolescents and
children (this review only included the data from adolescents) and five studies included adolescents
and adults. Detection of rifampicin resistance was assessed in 11 studies including two studies on
Truenat MTB-RIF Dx (Gomathi 2020a; Penn Nicholson 2021).

labels.text: Methodological quality
Figure 4 summarises the results of the risk of bias and applicability assessment for each of the
included studies.
The following studies were assessed as “high” risk of bias and/or applicability concern:
● Aguilera-Alonso 2022 - Patient selection, applicability concern; Reference standard
applicability concern based on recruitment of participants exclusively from tertiary referral
hospitals and lack of speciation of mycobacteria isolated in culture.
● Jose 2024 - Reference standard, high risk of bias; Patient selection, applicability concern
based on the reference standard was not blinded and participants were recruited from the
inpatient setting of a tertiary care hospital.
● Liu 2021- Patient selection, applicability concern based on inclusion criteria. Clinical
symptoms were not an inclusion criterion, whereas radiographic abnormalities were.
● MacLean 2023 - Patient selection, high risk of bias as study enrolled a convenience sample
and excluded those with recent COVID-19.
● Mishra 2020b - Patient selection, high risk of bias as the cohort was exclusively people with a
history of treated TB in the past 2 years.
● Opota 2019 - Patient selection, applicability concern based on exclusive inclusion of
hospitalized patients (tertiary hospital) with the goal of determining the need for airborne
isolation.
● Park 2019 - Patient selection, applicability concern based on recruitment of inpatients
exclusively from tertiary referral hospital.
● Piersimoni 2019 - Patient selection, applicability concern based on recruitment of inpatients
from tertiary referral hospital (<10% of participants were outpatients)
● Wang 2019 - Patient selection, high risk of bias; Patient selection, applicability concern based
on pre-selection for smear-negative participants and exclusive enrolment of inpatients at
tertiary referral hospital.

● For sputum, sensitivity was 75.3% (95% CI 68.9 to 80.8) and specificity was 95.9% (95% CI
92.3 to 97.9) in children 0 to 9 years, against MRS.
● For sputum, sensitivity was 70.4% (95% CI 56.0 to 81.7) and specificity was 95.6%  (95% CI
89.9 to 98.2) in children 0 to 9 years living with HIV, against MRS.
● For gastric aspirate, sensitivity was 69.6% (95% CI 60.3 to 77.6) and specificity was 91.0%
(95% CI 82.5 to 95.6) in children 0 to 9 years, against MRS.

97.5% (95% CI 95.1 to 98.7) in children 0 to 9 years, against MRS.

for nasopharyngeal aspirate to 48.8% for gastric aspirate specimens.

● Four studies assessed extrapulmonary tuberculosis. The largest population had CSF tested by

Discussion
Our review included 27 studies that assessed pulmonary TB and three studies assessed
extrapulmonary TB. The estimated summary sensitivity (95% CI) was 84.1% (78.3 to 88.6) and the
summary specificity was 96.1% (94.2 to 97.4) for the detection of pulmonary TB (18297 participants;
26 studies). The summary sensitivity of TB-LAMP for detection of pulmonary TB was lower [84.1%
(78.3 to 88.6)] than that of Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra [90.9% (86.2 to 94.7)] reported in a systematic
review of the accuracy of Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra (Zifodya 2021). In contrast the summary specificity of
TB-LAMP [96.1% (94.2 to 97.4)] was similar to that of Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra [95.6% (93.0 to 97.4)].
For detection of lymph node TB, the summary sensitivity (95% CI) was 94.3% (79.8 to 98.6) and the
summary specificity was 90.0% (79.5 to 95.4) from three studies (95 participants). Due to the paucity
of data, we did not perform meta-analyses of extrapulmonary TB involving other sites.
TB-LAMP's inability to detect rifampicin resistance is one of its limitations. Considering the ease of its
operation in resource-constrained settings, TB-LAMP could be a potential alternative for smear
microscopy and other mWRDs that necessitate complex infrastructure.

Patient selection
Risk of bias
Of the total 29 studies, 16 (55%) had high or unclear risk of bias as they either did prior testing before
including specimens in the study or used convenience sampling or the method of participant selection
was not reported.
Applicability concern
Only 45% of the studies were conducted in high TB/MDR TB burden country.
Index test
As all the index test assays were automated and thresholds were pre-defined, there is no scope of
subjective interpretation of results. We judged all of them at low concern for any risk of bias.
Reference Standard
Of the 29 studies, 9 (31%) had high or unclear risk of bias because either the results of the reference

Description of the articles found in the primary review (specific TBST)
Eight economic evaluations were conducted from middle-income countries (Russia and Brazil), these mostly
compared DiaskinTest against PPD-TST (Table A2, supplementary). One study met most of the Drummond’s
checklist factors and reported all the required information. Steffen et al (2020) 12 studied the cost-effectiveness
of two novel TBST (Diaskintest and C-TST) for people living with HIV (PLHIV) in Brazil compared to PPD-TST and
QFT-GIT. A Markov model was used to compare single screening strategies of the respective tests. The primary
outcome used was incremental cost-effectiveness ratio (ICER) per incremental gain in quality-adjusted life
years (QALY).
The rest of the articles came from Russia and were primarily focused on children using Diaskintest as an
alternative strategy to PPD-TST. Most of these studies included cost-effectiveness analyses using the ICER (per
case averted or diagnosed) as measure of effectiveness. The type of model used, time horizon, discounting
rate, and sensitivity analyses were either uncertain or not stated in the majority of these articles which might
bias the results of the studies 13-17.

The model describes the following states and steps in the TB infection care cascade: (1) no tuberculosis infection, tested; (2)
tuberculosis infection, tested; (3) no tuberculosis infection, treated; (4) no tuberculosis infection, untreated; (5) no
tuberculosis infection, treatment started but interrupted; (6) tuberculosis infection, treated; (7) tuberculosis infection,
untreated; (8) tuberculosis infection, treatment started but interrupted; (9) active TB; (10) no TB; (11) death. We start with
a cohort of individuals without TB.
Model parameters
The probabilities of moving between states are presented in Table 1. We initialise the model by
assuming 100,000 people without active TB (of all ages) get tested for TB infection and we follow
them through the cascade with a time horizon of 20 years (20 annual cycles). All parameters are
sourced from the literature. However, sensitivity and specificity of tests are informed by Objective 1
and are included as probabilities of being true positive (tpos), false negative (1-tpos), true negative
(tneg) and false positive (1-tneg). TBST specificity is currently assumed to be equal to that of the IGRA
(QuantiFERON-T Gold In-Tube).  All individuals in the model are assumed to belong to the general
population with TBI infection including TB case contacts, immunocompromised populations, among
other vulnerable groups. Differentiation between HIV status or time since infection are not included
in the model but Table B2 shows how the parametrisation of the model could be modified to account
for different populations, progression rates to active disease and infection duration.

labels.text: Figure 2. Incremental cost-effectiveness planes of DiaskinTest versus PPD-TST (blue), and DiaskinTest versus IGRA (green),
in Brazil, South Africa and UK. These figures show scatter plots of 1,000 Monte Carlo simulations for the mean incremental
costs and incremental effectiveness in quality-adjusted life years.
South Africa
Strategy 1 was cost saving compared to both strategy 2 and 3 (Figure 2). Compared to PPD-TST, DiaskinTest
was cost-saving at $4.39 with an incremental gain of 0.0152 QALYs. Compared to IGRA, DiaskinTest was cost
saving at $64.41 with an incremental gain of 0.0065 QALYs. As the intervention was cost saving, we calculated
incremental net benefit (INB) rather than incremental cost-effective ratio (Table 5). Scenario analysis on cost of
the test show that, with same sensitivity and specificity values as DiaskinTest, the DiaskinTest would remain
cost saving compared to PPD-TST for an increase in unit cost of the test up to approximatively $9 compared to
the unit cost of DiaskinTest. Meaning, a test unit cost of $99.93 would lead to an average expected cost per
patient equal to PPD-TST’s ($64.89). Scenario analysis on number of tests performed, shows that in the worst-
case scenario of only one test being performed with one DiaskinTest vial, the expected cost of the strategy in
South Africa would then be $68.73, making the strategy no longer cost saving. However, the strategy would still
be cost-effective when comparing its cost per QUALY of $427.83 with South Africa’s willingness to pay
threshold of $4,71416.
